issues.legal_issue: Under the customary law governing the community, a daughter is preferred to collaterals in succession to non-ancestral property.
material_facts: The dispute concerned property inherited by a widow from her husband, part of which was found to be non-ancestral.

The parties relied on a customary-law compilation stating that a daughter is preferred to collaterals in respect of her father's acquired property, and on a settlement record stating generally that daughters did not succeed under any circumstances.
The settlement record did not distinguish ancestral from non-ancestral property, and the Court found no clear indication that the question or answer covered non-ancestral property.
The oral evidence was insufficient to establish a custom preferring collaterals to daughters for non-ancestral property.
issues.conclusion: The daughter is preferred to collaterals in succession to the non-ancestral property; the settlement-record entry did not establish a contrary custom for that property.
issues.legal_principle: Under paragraph 23 of Rattigan's Digest of Customary Law, daughters are preferred to collaterals in succession to acquired property. Under section 35 of the Evidence Act, entries in a Riwaj-i-am are relevant and ordinarily carry a presumption of correctness; that presumption is weak where the entry adversely affects females who had no opportunity to appear, as explained in Mt. Subhani v. Nawab. A general question and answer in a Riwaj-i-am ordinarily relates to ancestral property unless there is a clear indication otherwise. The Court approved Mt. Hurmate v. Hoshiaru and disapproved Mohinder Singh v. Kher Singh; earlier decisions relying on the contrary interpretation of the entry did not establish the custom.

rule.if: customary_succession_dispute and property_is_non_ancestral and settlement_question_is_general and no_clear_indication_of_non_ancestral_property and no_independent_proof_of_collateral_preference

predicates.customary_succession_dispute: The case concerns succession under a community's customary law.
predicates.property_is_non_ancestral: The property in dispute was not ancestral property.
predicates.settlement_question_is_general: The recorded customary-law question and answer did not distinguish between ancestral and non-ancestral property.
predicates.no_clear_indication_of_non_ancestral_pro: The recorded question and answer did not clearly show that they addressed non-ancestral property.
predicates.no_independent_proof_of_collateral_prefe: Evidence apart from the general settlement entry did not establish that collaterals were preferred to daughters for non-ancestral property.

issues.definition: When a customary-succession dispute concerns non-ancestral property and a general settlement entry does not clearly address that property or establish a contrary custom, the daughter is preferred to collaterals.

issues.legal_issue: A widow's gift of only part of the property in which she holds a limited estate does not accelerate the reversion by surrender.
material_facts: The widow held a limited estate in property that included both ancestral and non-ancestral land.
She gifted the non-ancestral property to her daughters, who were reversioners in respect of that property, but the daughters were not reversioners in respect of the ancestral property.
The deed also concerned property given to persons who were not reversioners as to that property, and property was retained by the widow; the house was not included in the gift.
The gift was not a surrender of the widow's entire interest in the entire property.
issues.conclusion: The gift did not accelerate the daughters' succession and was not valid beyond the widow's lifetime.
issues.legal_principle: The Hindu-law doctrine of surrender rests on the limited owner's complete self-effacement in favour of the reversioner. To accelerate the reversion, the surrender must cover the limited owner's entire interest in the entire property; the law does not recognize partial self-effacement or separate effacement as to ancestral and non-ancestral property. Retaining a small portion for maintenance does not relax the rule. The Court relied on Rangaswami Gounden v. Nachiappa Gounden and Phool Kaur v. Prem Kaur.

rule.if: challenge_to_widow_gift and widow_held_limited_estate and gift_benefited_only_some_reversioners and widow_did_not_transfer_entire_interest_in_entire_property

predicates.challenge_to_widow_gift: The proceeding challenged a gift made by a widow who held a limited estate.
predicates.widow_held_limited_estate: The widow held a limited interest in the property before making the gift.
predicates.gift_benefited_only_some_reversioners: The gift benefited persons who were reversioners as to only part of the property covered by the widow's estate.
predicates.widow_did_not_transfer_entire_interest_i: The widow did not surrender her entire interest in the entire property, whether because property was retained or because some property was transferred to persons who were not reversioners as to it.

issues.definition: When a widow holding a limited estate makes a gift that benefits only some reversioners and does not transfer her entire interest in the entire property, the gift does not accelerate the reversion.

issues.legal_issue: A newly raised statutory ownership claim that depends on unresolved possession facts should not be determined in an appeal on a record lacking evidence of those facts.
material_facts: A claim under the statutory provision concerning a female Hindu's full ownership was raised for the first time in the appeal after the lower courts had decided the suit.
The parties had not adduced evidence directed to the statutory claim.
The record did not establish whether the widow was in actual or constructive possession, or whether the daughters possessed the property permissively or independently.
The appellants did not clarify the relevant possession circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to determine the statutory ownership claim in the appeal and left the parties to raise it in a future suit if so advised.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act was invoked, but the Court expressed no view on the claim's merits. It held that the claim should not be considered on an incomplete record when the possession facts material to its application had not been tried or established; those factual and legal questions could be considered in a future suit.

rule.if: appeal_from_final_decree and new_statutory_ownership_claim and claim_not_raised_in_lower_courts and material_possession_facts_not_in_evidence

predicates.appeal_from_final_decree: The proceeding was an appeal from a final decree in a suit.
predicates.new_statutory_ownership_claim: A party advanced a statutory claim to full ownership for the first time in the appeal.
predicates.claim_not_raised_in_lower_courts: The statutory claim had not been raised before the lower courts disposed of the suit.
predicates.material_possession_facts_not_in_evidenc: The record lacked evidence establishing possession circumstances material to the statutory claim.

issues.definition: When a new statutory ownership claim is raised in an appeal and material possession facts were not established in the lower-court record, the claim is left for determination in a later suit.
